title: OWASP API security top 10 (practical ASP.NET Core mitigations)
hook: The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) API Security Top 10 lists the most common ways APIs get breached. ASP.NET Core gives you middleware and patterns to mitigate each — if you apply them deliberately.

blocks.text: OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) covers broken object level authorization (BOLA), broken authentication, unrestricted resource consumption, and more. For ASP.NET Core Web APIs, mitigations map to policy handlers, rate limiting, input validation, Problem Details without stack leaks, and secure token handling. This topic ties auth concepts from the module to a checklist senior engineers use in design reviews and interviews.

entries.plainDefinition: API allows access to another user's object by changing id in URL — #1 API risk.
entries.example: GET /orders/999 when 999 belongs to another tenant

entries.plainDefinition: User accesses admin function without admin role — missing [Authorize(Policy)].
Default credentials, verbose errors, open CORS, missing HTTPS.
No rate limits or pagination — DoS via expensive endpoints.

blocks.text: FAANG and product company security interviews ask you to walk through OWASP API items with concrete ASP.NET Core controls — not vague 'we use HTTPS.' BOLA alone causes most API breaches because developers authenticate users but skip resource-level authorization. Mapping Top 10 to JwtBearer, IAuthorizationHandler, AddRateLimiter, and [AllowAnonymous] discipline shows production maturity.

blocks.title: AuthN without AuthZ is incomplete
blocks.body: API2 Broken Authentication and API1 BOLA overlap with this module — valid JWT does not mean user may access object id in the route.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: OWASP API Top 10 → ASP.NET Core mitigation map

items.title: API1 BOLA
items.body: Resource-based IAuthorizationHandler; never trust client-supplied ids without ownership check.

items.title: API2 Broken authentication
items.body: JwtBearer validation, short TTL, refresh rotation, no password grant; lockout via IdP.

items.title: API3 Broken object property level authorization
items.body: DTOs with read/write separation; avoid returning entity with sensitive fields.

items.title: API4 Unrestricted resource consumption
items.body: AddRateLimiter, pagination caps, request size limits, timeouts.

items.title: API5–API10
items.body: BFLA → policies; misconfiguration → hardened Program.cs; unsafe consumption → validate outbound URLs; supply chain → pinned packages.

diagram.title: Defense layers for a typical Web API
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  EDGE[Reverse proxy TLS WAF] --> RL[Rate limiter]
  RL --> AUTHN[JWT / API key AuthN]
  AUTHN --> AUTHZ[Policy + resource handlers\nBOLA BFLA]
  AUTHZ --> VAL[Validation filters]
  VAL --> APP[Business logic]
  APP --> ERR[Problem Details\nno stack leak]

snippet.label: BOLA mitigation — resource authorization
snippet.explanation: API1 fix: load resource, authorize against it. Team policy chooses 404 vs 403 for non-owned ids — document consistently.

snippet.label: Rate limiting and request size (API4)
snippet.explanation: Rate limit by user or IP; cap body size to reduce upload DoS. Return 429 with Retry-After header in production.

snippet.label: Security headers and hardened production config (API8)
snippet.explanation: Misconfiguration: permissive CORS, developer exception page in prod, missing HSTS. Problem Details replaces stack traces for API clients.

snippet.label: Audit logging for security events (production proof)
snippet.explanation: Detect BOLA probing (403 bursts on sequential ids), credential stuffing (401 spikes), abuse (429). Never log Bearer tokens or API keys.

blocks.title: OWASP mitigations in Node vs ASP.NET Core
Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Only global [Authorize] without per-resource checks (BOLA). Swagger UI exposed in production without auth. CORS AllowAnyOrigin with credentials. Logging Authorization headers. Using int sequential ids without tenant scoping in multi-tenant APIs.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: run OWASP ZAP or API security CI against staging with auth tokens. Application Insights alerts on 403 rate per user scanning id ranges. dotnet-counters for thread-pool queue length when API4 attacks hit unbounded endpoints. Pen test findings mapped to GitHub issues with policy handler tests in WebApplicationFactory proving BOLA fixes.

blocks.title: OWASP API Top 10 quick mitigation reference
rows: Resource IAuthorizationHandler; tenant filter in EF
HSTS, CORS lockdown, no dev page in prod

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Naming OWASP Top 10 web instead of API list. Saying HTTPS alone secures APIs. Cannot explain BOLA with a concrete id-in-URL example. No mention of rate limiting or resource-level authorization.

interviewTakeaways: OWASP API Top 10 #1 is BOLA — fix with resource authorization, not just [Authorize].
Combine JwtBearer, policies, rate limiting, CORS discipline, and Problem Details without stack leaks.
Production tip: security audit logs on 401/403/429; ZAP in CI; alert on id enumeration patterns.
60s: Authenticate with JWT or API key. Authorize with policies plus resource handlers for object ids. Rate limit. Harden Program.cs. Never log tokens. BOLA is the breach leaders see most.
Follow-up: 404 vs 403 when object exists but user lacks access?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'we use JWT so OWASP auth is covered' gets you rejected — JWT is API2 enabler not fix; validation and AuthZ still required.
Global admin role check only — BFLA and BOLA need endpoint and object-level policies.
Strong answer: 'I map each OWASP API item: BOLA resource handler, API4 rate limiter, API8 no dev exception in prod, audit 403 spikes for enumeration.'
